name: Macedonian Empire
summary: Alexander the Great’s empire, built in barely a decade from Greece to India. It split into rival Hellenistic kingdoms soon after his death in 323 BCE.

knownFor.label: Alexander the Great
knownFor.note: Conquered from Greece to India in about a decade.

knownFor.label: Alexandria
knownFor.note: The most famous of the cities he founded, later home of the Great Library.

location.value: From Macedon in northern Greece to Egypt, Persia and the Indus valley under Alexander the Great.

terrain.value: Mountains and plains in Macedon, then the whole former Persian Empire: deserts, river valleys and mountain ranges.
terrain.source: Bosworth, Conquest and Empire: The Reign of Alexander the Great (1988)

climate.value: From Mediterranean to desert and monsoon India.

resources.value: Macedonian timber, gold and silver (from Thracian mines), then the vast Persian treasuries.

disasters.value: Not documented in the sources checked.

population.value: Not given in Wikipedia. Alexander’s empire ruled many millions of people across the former Persian lands.

urbanisation.value: Capitals Aigai and Pella. Alexander founded many cities, most famously Alexandria in Egypt (331 BCE).

disease.value: Alexander died in Babylon in 323 BCE, possibly of illness. The cause is debated.
disease.source: Bosworth, Conquest and Empire: The Reign of Alexander the Great (1988)

migration.value: Greek and Macedonian settlers moved into new cities across Asia. Alexander encouraged marriages with Persian women.

economicBase.value: Agriculture and mining in Macedon, then tribute and seized Persian treasure.

tradeRoutes.value: Connected the Mediterranean, Mesopotamia and India, opening the Hellenistic trade world.
tradeRoutes.source: Bosworth, Conquest and Empire: The Reign of Alexander the Great (1988)

wealth.value: Seizing Persian treasuries made it enormously rich. There is no GDP estimate.
wealth.source: Bosworth, Conquest and Empire: The Reign of Alexander the Great (1988)

moneyAndTax.value: Silver tetradrachms with Alexander’s image became a standard coinage across the Hellenistic world.

inequality.value: The king and Macedonian nobles (Companions) above soldiers, subjects and slaves.
inequality.source: Bosworth, Conquest and Empire: The Reign of Alexander the Great (1988)

governmentType.value: A hereditary monarchy: a near-absolute king (basileus) with an assembly of the army and nobles.

keyRulers.value: Philip II (359–336 BCE). Alexander the Great (336–323 BCE). After 323 BCE his generals (the Diadochi) divided the empire.

succession.value: Hereditary but violent: Philip II was assassinated (336 BCE). Alexander died without an adult heir, and his generals fought over the empire.

institutions.value: The League of Corinth (338–337 BCE) united the Greek cities under Macedon. Alexander kept many Persian administrative practices (satrapies).

stability.value: Short-lived: rebellions in Greece (the Lamian War, 323–322 BCE) and the Wars of the Diadochi (322–272 BCE) after Alexander’s death.

eliteConflict.value: Tension between Alexander and his Macedonian officers over adopting Persian customs. Generals competed for power after 323 BCE.
eliteConflict.source: Bosworth, Conquest and Empire: The Reign of Alexander the Great (1988)

armyAndTech.value: The Macedonian phalanx with long sarissa spears, the Companion cavalry and skilled siege engineers.

majorWars.value: Chaeronea (338 BCE). Alexander’s victories at the Granicus (334), Issus (333) and Gaugamela (331 BCE). The campaign to India (Hydaspes, 326 BCE).

territoryChange.value: About 5.2 million km² by 323 BCE (Wikipedia infobox), conquered in about ten years.

alliancesRivals.value: Rivals: Athens and Thebes, the Achaemenid Persian Empire, and Indian kings such as Porus.

inventions.value: Advanced siege engines and torsion catapults.
inventions.source: Bosworth, Conquest and Empire: The Reign of Alexander the Great (1988)

scienceEducation.value: Aristotle tutored Alexander. Alexander’s expedition included scholars who collected knowledge of plants, animals and geography.

openness.value: Alexander blended Greek and Persian customs and administration.

religion.value: Greek polytheism. Alexander was honoured as a god in Egypt (visiting the oracle of Siwa).
religion.source: Bosworth, Conquest and Empire: The Reign of Alexander the Great (1988)

languageWriting.value: Ancient Macedonian and Greek. Koine Greek became the common language of the Hellenistic world.

artsArchitecture.value: The royal tombs at Aigai (Vergina), mosaics at Pella, and Alexander’s portraits.

socialStructure.value: King, nobles (hetairoi), free farmers and soldiers, and slaves.

sharedIdentity.value: Loyalty to the king and army. Alexander tried to create a mixed Greek–Persian elite.
sharedIdentity.source: Bosworth, Conquest and Empire: The Reign of Alexander the Great (1988)

neighbours.value: Greek city-states, Thrace, Illyria, the Persian Empire, Egypt and Indian kingdoms.

ideasReligions.value: Began the Hellenistic age: Greek language, art and ideas spread from Egypt to Central Asia and India.

colonisation.value: A conquering empire that founded Greek cities (many named Alexandria) across Asia.

riseSignals.value: Philip II’s army reforms and diplomacy, Thracian gold, and victory over the Greek cities (338 BCE).

peakPeriod.value: At Alexander’s death in 323 BCE, briefly the most powerful empire in the world.

declineSignals.value: Alexander’s early death without an adult heir, and rivalry among his generals.

outcome.value: Fragmentation into the Hellenistic kingdoms (Seleucid, Ptolemaic and Antigonid Macedon). Rome conquered Macedon after the Battle of Pydna (168 BCE).

sources.value: Later Greek and Roman historians (Arrian, Plutarch, Diodorus), coins and inscriptions. Checked against Wikipedia on 6 Nov 2026. See also Bosworth (1988). This entry covers Alexander’s empire; the kingdom of Macedon lasted c. 7th century–168 BCE.

overallCertainty.value: Good for the campaigns. Many details come from writers living centuries later, and the cause of Alexander’s death is debated. Second source: Wikidata covers the whole ancient kingdom of Macedonia (808–167 BCE); this app covers Alexander’s empire (336–323 BCE).
